sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll have Tabnine installed, understand its privacy guarantee and why it matters to specific industries, and have a clear sense of when it's the right tool — and when it isn't.

## What is Tabnine?

Tabnine is an AI code completion tool that has been around since 2018 — longer than Copilot, Cody, or any of the tools we've covered in this part. Its longevity is not an accident. Tabnine has stayed relevant by building around a guarantee that no other major tool offers: **your code never has to leave your machine**.

Every other AI coding tool in this course — Copilot, Cody, Continue.dev with Claude, Cursor, Aider — sends your code to a cloud server to generate suggestions. Tabnine can do that too (and offers a cloud mode), but it can also run **entirely locally** using a model downloaded to your computer.

For most developers, this doesn't matter much. But for some, it's non-negotiable.

**Who actually needs local AI?** If you work in healthcare (patient data), finance (trading algorithms, client data), legal (privileged communications), government (classified work), or any org with a strict IP policy about code leaving the network — Tabnine's local mode is worth knowing about. These industries have real liability exposure if code snippets are sent to third-party cloud servers.

## How Tabnine's Privacy Model Works

Tabnine has three deployment modes:

**1. Cloud mode (free and Pro tiers)**
Suggestions are generated by Tabnine's cloud servers. Code snippets are sent for processing. Fast, capable, uses large models.

**2. Local mode (Pro tier)**
A smaller AI model (~1–2 GB) runs entirely on your machine. No code is ever transmitted. Suggestions may be slightly less sophisticated than cloud mode, but they work offline and in air-gapped environments.

**3. Enterprise (self-hosted)**
Tabnine's server runs inside your organisation's infrastructure. Full control. Compliant with the strictest enterprise security policies.

For this lesson, you'll install the free tier and explore what the settings look like.

## Installing Tabnine in VS Code

1. Open VS Code Extensions (`Ctrl+Shift+X`)
2. Search **"Tabnine"**
3. Install **Tabnine: AI Autocomplete & Chat for Javascript, Python, Typescript, PHP, Go, Java & more** — the one by Tabnine
4. Click **Sign up** in the Tabnine sidebar and create a free account at tabnine.com

Once signed in, Tabnine activates automatically. You'll see inline suggestions appear as you type — greyed-out text, just like Copilot. Press `Tab` to accept.

## Team Mode — Learning Your Patterns

One of Tabnine's enterprise features is worth understanding even if you don't use it today.

In **Team mode**, Tabnine trains a supplementary model on your team's actual codebase. Over time, it starts suggesting code that matches your team's specific patterns — your naming conventions, your preferred function structures, your internal libraries. It doesn't just know JavaScript; it knows *your team's* JavaScript.

This is the "private by default, personalised at scale" pitch. The model is trained internally, never shared outside the org, and improves as the team writes more code.

For a solo learner this isn't relevant yet. But if you end up at a company using Tabnine, this is the feature that makes it more than just a generic autocomplete.

## Tabnine vs Copilot — Honest Comparison

It's worth being direct here. For general coding use, GitHub Copilot's suggestions are currently stronger. Tabnine's advantage is not capability — it's the privacy guarantee.

| | Tabnine | GitHub Copilot |
|---|---|---|
| Suggestion quality | Good | Excellent |
| Local / offline mode | Yes (Pro) | No |
| Code stays on your machine | Yes (local mode) | No |
| Team pattern learning | Yes (Enterprise) | Limited |
| Free tier | Yes | Yes |
| Price (Pro) | $12/user/mo | $10/user/mo |
| Works in air-gapped environments | Yes | No |

**Choose Tabnine when:** privacy is a requirement, not a preference. Your code cannot leave your network. You're in a regulated industry or working under a strict IP agreement.

**Choose Copilot when:** you want the best suggestions on general coding tasks and privacy is not a blocker.

The key insight: Tabnine and Copilot are not competing on the same dimension. Tabnine is the answer to a different question.

**Conflict note:** Like Cody, Tabnine can conflict with Copilot if both are suggesting completions at the same time. If you're testing Tabnine alongside Copilot, consider disabling one's inline completions while evaluating the other. Both can coexist — just configure them so they're not fighting for the same cursor.

sections.title: Install Tabnine and Explore Its Privacy Settings
sections.content:
**Goal:** Install Tabnine, activate it, compare its completions to Copilot, and find its privacy configuration options.

**Step 1 — Install:**
1. Open VS Code Extensions (`Ctrl+Shift+X`)
2. Search `Tabnine` → install the extension
3. Sign up for a free account when prompted

**Step 2 — Test completions:**
1. Open `exercises/practice.js`
2. Go to the bottom of the file and start typing a new function:
```
// Function to check if a string is a valid email address
function isValidEmail(
```
3. Pause after the opening parenthesis — wait for Tabnine's greyed-out suggestion to appear
4. Press `Tab` to accept it
5. Now compare: how does this feel vs Copilot? More conservative? Different style?

**Step 3 — Explore the privacy settings:**
1. Click the Tabnine icon in the VS Code Status Bar (bottom, usually shows a small T icon)
2. Select **Settings** or open the Tabnine extension settings via `Ctrl+,` and search `Tabnine`
3. Look for the privacy-related settings — note options like `Keep my code private` and telemetry controls
4. You don't need to change anything — just understand what's configurable

**Step 4 — Reflect:**
Write 3 sentences answering: in what situation would you choose Tabnine over Copilot for a real project?

Guide for your answer: think about regulated industries, client work with strict IP clauses, or any scenario where "no code leaves the machine" is a requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

**What to observe:** Tabnine works, and works well. Its suggestions are competent. The privacy settings exist and are accessible. For the specific use cases it's designed for, it's not a compromise — it's the right tool.

sections.title: Workshop A — Privacy-First AI Coding Assessment
sections.content:
Understand the real privacy implications of different AI coding tools.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"Compare the data privacy approaches of these AI coding tools: GitHub Copilot, Claude Code (Anthropic API), Tabnine, and local models (e.g., Ollama). For each: what data is sent to their servers, what is their retention policy, and when would an organisation require this option over others?"*

**Step 2 — Identify your privacy requirements:** Do you work with code that contains:
- Proprietary algorithms that cannot leave your infrastructure
- Client data or PII in code or comments
- Security vulnerabilities that shouldn't be sent to external services
- Regulated data (healthcare, financial)

**Step 3 — Map your requirements to the right tool:** For each type of code you write, which AI tool is appropriate?

**Step 4 — Write a personal AI privacy policy** for your coding workflow.

sections.title: Workshop B — Test Tabnine for Your Real Codebase
sections.content:
Evaluate Tabnine's practical value for your specific coding context.

**Step 1 — Install Tabnine** in VS Code (Extensions marketplace).

**Step 2 — Complete at least 30 minutes of real coding** with Tabnine active. Use it on code from your actual project, not toy examples.

**Step 3 — Track these metrics:**
- How often do you accept a Tabnine suggestion? (count)
- How often is the suggestion exactly right? (0-10 per hour)
- How often is it close but wrong? (needs editing)
- How often is it completely wrong? (you ignore it)

**Step 4 — Compare to another AI tool** on the same task (Claude Code or Copilot). Are the completions better or worse?

**Step 5 — For privacy-sensitive code**, run a task that would normally be too sensitive for Copilot. Does Tabnine's local-first approach address your concern?

sections.title: Workshop C — Local AI Models for Privacy
sections.content:
Explore the option of running AI coding assistance entirely locally with no data leaving your machine.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"Explain how local AI coding models work (e.g., running Ollama with CodeLlama or Mistral). What are the trade-offs vs cloud AI coding tools in terms of: code quality, speed, privacy, cost, and setup complexity?"*

**Step 2 — Assess if local models are right for you:**
- Do you have a GPU? (significant performance difference)
- How sensitive is your code?
- Is occasional slower/lower quality assistance acceptable?

**Step 3 — If appropriate, try Ollama:**
Install Ollama (ollama.ai) and run: `ollama pull codellama:7b`
Connect it to Continue.dev as a local model.

**Step 4 — Compare local vs cloud** on a coding task. How much does quality differ? Is the privacy gain worth it for your use case?

sections.title: Workshop D — Build Your Tiered AI Tool Policy
sections.content:
Create a tiered policy matching code sensitivity to the right AI tool.

**Step 1 — Categorise your code by sensitivity:**
- Tier 1 (Public/open source): Can use any cloud AI tool
- Tier 2 (Internal business logic): Cloud AI acceptable with standard terms
- Tier 3 (Proprietary algorithms/client data): Require privacy-first tool (Tabnine local, local model)
- Tier 4 (Regulated/classified): No AI assistance without explicit approval

**Step 2 — Assign each tier to a tool:**
| Tier | AI Tool | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Claude Code / Copilot | No privacy concern |
| 2 | Claude Code | API terms acceptable |
| 3 | Tabnine local / Ollama | Data stays local |
| 4 | Manual / approved tool | Too sensitive |

**Step 3 — Adapt the tiers** to your specific work context.

**Step 4 — Share with your team** as a starting point for a team-wide AI coding policy.

sections.question: Tabnine's main privacy claim is that it can run entirely locally. What does this mean for your code?
options: Your code is never analysed or used for any purpose
Your code (for completions) is processed only on your machine — it is not sent to Tabnine's servers, so it cannot be used to train models or be seen by Tabnine's staff
Your code is encrypted before being sent to Tabnine
Tabnine's local model is as accurate as cloud models
sections.explanation: Local processing means the code used for generating completions never leaves your machine. This addresses the primary concern with cloud AI tools: that your proprietary code becomes training data or is accessible to the vendor's staff. The trade-off: local models are typically less capable than the large cloud models. For sensitive codebases where privacy is the primary concern, this trade-off is often worthwhile.

sections.question: Your company has a policy that "no proprietary code may be sent to third-party AI services." Which coding AI tool can you use without violating this policy?
options: GitHub Copilot — it has strong privacy guarantees
Any tool where completions are processed entirely locally without sending code to external servers
Claude Code — Anthropic has strong data protection
Any tool that signs a data processing agreement
sections.explanation: The policy requirement is that code cannot be sent to third-party services, regardless of their privacy guarantees or contractual protections. The only tools that definitively satisfy this are those that process code entirely locally: local models (Ollama + CodeLlama), Tabnine with local mode enabled, or any self-hosted AI model. Cloud tools like Copilot, Claude Code, and Codeium — even with strong privacy guarantees — technically send code to external servers.

sections.content: **Lesson complete.** Tabnine may not be your daily driver, but knowing it exists — and knowing exactly when it's the right call — is part of being a well-rounded AI practitioner. The best tool isn't always the most powerful one; it's the one that fits your constraints.
